sections.Astrophysical Alerts:
#### IceCube-261123A: no additional IceCube track excess; ZTF identifies a pre-existing supernova-like counterpart candidate

IceCube’s **Bronze** track candidate was detected on **23 November 2026 at 06:54:16.990 UTC**; its revised direction is **RA 320.45°, Dec +24.58°** (J2000), with 90% PSF-containment uncertainties of about 1.4°–1.7°, an energy estimator of **145 TeV**, signalness **0.457**, and atmospheric-background false-alarm rate **1.205 yr⁻¹** ([GCN 46345](https://gcn.nasa.gov/circulars/46345)). It remains a candidate event, not a source identification.

A follow-up released **25 November 2026 at 16:05:09 UTC** found zero additional track-like events, excluding the alert itself, inside the 90% region in the ±500 s window; the reported p-value is **1.00**. The corresponding two-day search, from **22 November 06:54:16.990 UTC to 24 November 06:54:16.990 UTC**, also has p = 1.00. IceCube quotes point-source *sensitivities*—not measured fluxes—at 1 TeV of **1.4 × 10⁻¹** and **1.7 × 10⁻¹ GeV cm⁻²** for an assumed E⁻²·⁵ spectrum in the 1000 s and two-day windows, respectively ([GCN 46367](https://gcn.nasa.gov/circulars/46367)).

ZTF began g/r imaging at **24 November 01:35 UTC**, 18.7 h after the neutrino, covering **82.6% (5.3 deg²)** of the reported region to a typical **21.0 mag** depth. Its pipeline retained **ZTF26accqpcr / AT 2026ahvn**, at RA **320.8718982°**, Dec **+25.3739940°**, r = **19.29 ± 0.05** on the report’s observation. However, it was first detected on **20 October**, approximately a month before the neutrino; it brightened then faded and reddened. The authors flag it as a potentially interesting CSM-interacting-supernova candidate conditional on spectroscopic confirmation, not as an established counterpart ([GCN 46370](https://gcn.nasa.gov/circulars/46370)). Temporal coincidence is therefore not evidence of association.

#### GRB 261122B: a well-localized, long, multi-pulse burst with optical afterglow

SVOM/ECLAIRs triggered on **22 November 2026 at 22:46:55 UTC**. The refined ECLAIRs analysis reported **25 November at 10:49:26 UTC** finds three bright peaks and **T₉₀ = 222.8 ± 1.8 s** in 4–120 keV. The pre-slew (T₀+2.7 to +37 s) power-law fit has index **−1.70 ± 0.12** and fluence **(7.23 ± 0.83) × 10⁻⁷ erg cm⁻²**; the post-slew interval (T₀+156 to +226 s) is softer, index **−2.37 ± 0.04**, with **(1.70 ± 0.05) × 10⁻⁶ erg cm⁻²**. These are 68%-confidence spectral-fit errors ([GCN 46365](https://gcn.nasa.gov/circulars/46365)).

A contemporaneous SVOM/GRM reduction, reported **25 November at 20:43 UTC**, gives **T₉₀ = 193⁺¹⁰₋₉ s** in 15–5000 keV. With the precise SVOM/VT optical position **RA 3.97°, Dec −38.83°** (0.50 arcsec reported error), the broadband prompt fit has **Eₚₑₐₖ = 58.7⁺²¹·⁸₋₁₁·⁴ keV**, index **−1.6⁺⁰·³₋₀·⁴**, and 10–1000 keV fluence **(7.15⁺¹·²²₋₀·₈₃) × 10⁻⁶ erg cm⁻²** ([GCN 46369](https://gcn.nasa.gov/circulars/46369)). GCN follow-ups have reported an optical counterpart, but the present reports provide neither a redshift nor an energetics-based progenitor inference.

#### GRB 261122A: long gamma-ray burst characterized by SVOM/GRM

GRB 261122A triggered SVOM/GRM and was also detected by Fermi/GBM at **22 November 2026, 01:32:22 UTC**. The GRM ground analysis was reported **25 November at 20:34:44 UTC**. It resolves a multi-pulse event with **T₉₀ = 93⁺¹⁸₋₂₃ s** (15–5000 keV), consistent with an operational long-GRB classification ([GCN 46368](https://gcn.nasa.gov/circulars/46368)).

For T₀−47 to T₀+73 s, a cutoff power law yields index **−1.5⁺⁰·²₋₀·³**, **Eₚₑₐₖ = 396⁺⁸⁵⁸₋₁₈₇ keV**, and 10–1000 keV fluence **(1.2 ± 0.2) × 10⁻⁵ erg cm⁻²**. The large asymmetric peak-energy uncertainty should not be over-interpreted. Fermi’s GBM localization is **RA 271.1°, Dec −57.7°**, with stated **3.7°** error; the field lay about **98°** from SVOM’s optical axis, outside ECLAIRs’ field of view. No counterpart, redshift, or physical source association is established by this prompt-emission report.

#### EP261122a: Einstein Probe observes rapid X-ray fading

Einstein Probe WXT detected EP261122a beginning **22 November 2026 at 06:09:52 UTC**, a single **170 s** X-ray pulse. The refined report, issued **25 November at 11:13:45 UTC**, fits the average 0.5–4 keV WXT spectrum with an absorbed power law, fixed Galactic N_H = **1.11 × 10²¹ cm⁻²**, photon index **1.30⁺⁰·⁴⁸₋₀·⁴⁵**, and unabsorbed flux **3.13⁺⁰·⁹⁹₋₀·⁸⁰ × 10⁻¹⁰ erg s⁻¹ cm⁻²** ([GCN 46366](https://gcn.nasa.gov/circulars/46366)).

FXT autonomously observed from **07:17:14 UTC** (T₀+4042 s), detecting an uncatalogued source at **RA 49.3135°, Dec +16.4448°** with a **10-arcsec, 90%-confidence** radius. Its 0.5–10 keV unabsorbed flux was **3.88⁺²·⁵⁰₋₁·³⁸ × 10⁻¹³ erg s⁻¹ cm⁻²**. A second FXT observation beginning **24 November 10:21:26 UTC** found no significant source and set a **90%** upper limit of **1.2 × 10⁻¹⁴ erg cm⁻² s⁻¹**, implying a decline of at least **32** relative to the first FXT epoch. This is strong transient behavior, but no source class, optical counterpart or redshift is supplied.
